title: Circuits
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT Physics, Mathematics and Research Reasoning lessons. Models and calculations use stated assumptions. Independent scientific review is pending; this is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Electric current is charge crossing a surface per time: I = ΔQ/Δt. One ampere is one coulomb per second.
Conventional current follows positive-charge flow. In a metal wire, electron drift is opposite conventional current; a complete circuit is needed for sustained steady current.
At a circuit junction, steady charge conservation gives total current in equal to total current out. Charge does not ordinarily accumulate indefinitely at an ideal junction.
Current is not consumed by a resistor. Energy is transferred as charges move through potential differences, while the steady series current is shared by all series elements.

steps.text: An ohmic resistor obeys V = IR over a specified regime. Resistance can depend on temperature, geometry and material; a linear relation is not universal for every device.
Series resistances add and carry the same current. Parallel branches share potential difference and have reciprocal resistances that add.
For a uniform wire, R = ρelectricalL/A. Electrical resistivity is not mass density. Lengthening a wire raises resistance, whereas increasing area lowers it.
Dissipated power is IV, or I²R and V²/R when Ohm’s law applies. Decide whether current or voltage is held fixed before predicting how a resistance change affects power.

steps.text: Capacitance relates stored charge magnitude to potential difference: C = Q/V. An ideal parallel-plate model gives C = κε0A/d, neglecting edge fields.
A dielectric increases capacitance for fixed plate geometry. What happens to charge and voltage depends on whether a battery remains connected or the capacitor is isolated.
Stored energy can be written ½CV², Q²/(2C) or ½QV. Increasing capacitance raises energy at fixed voltage but lowers energy at fixed charge.
An ideal capacitor blocks steady direct current after charging, although current flows during transients. The changing field stores energy without sustained conduction across the ideal dielectric.

steps.text: An ammeter measures current and is inserted in series with the branch of interest. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance so it does not appreciably alter that current.
A voltmeter measures potential difference across two points and is connected in parallel. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and draws no current.
A real meter can load a circuit. Placing a low-resistance ammeter directly across a source can create a dangerously high-current path; the schematic is an instructional model, not a wiring procedure.
Read the intended branch and connection before using a meter value. A voltmeter reading depends on both lead placement and the chosen polarity.
